fields.h1: The Life of Antony by Athanasius: Summary and Study Guide
fields.meta_title: The Life of Antony by Athanasius: Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A reader’s study guide to Athanasius’s Life of Antony — the founding biography of Christian monasticism. Summary, story, themes, and how to read it today.
fields.body_html:
The Life of Antony is Athanasius of Alexandria’s short fourth-century biography of Antony the Great, the Egyptian Christian who sold everything, walked into the desert, and became the father of Christian monasticism. In roughly forty brief chapters it tells one man’s life from a whispered gospel reading in a village church to a peaceful death at more than a hundred years old—and along the way it gave the whole church a picture of what wholehearted devotion could look like. If you want the summary in a sentence: it is the story of how a single act of obedience to ‘sell what you have’ emptied a young man of his fortune and filled him, over a lifetime, with God. This study guide walks you through what the book is, the story it tells, its central themes, who will profit from it, and how a modern reader can meet its very ancient spirituality with sympathy rather than suspicion.

What the book is — and who wrote it

The Life of Antony was written around A.D. 356–362, soon after Antony’s death, by Athanasius of Alexandria—the same bishop and theologian who fought so long for the full divinity of Christ that his opponents coined the phrase Athanasius contra mundum, ‘Athanasius against the world.’ Athanasius knew Antony personally; the book records that the aged hermit once travelled to Alexandria and that Athanasius himself escorted him from the city. This is not distant legend gathered centuries later, then, but a portrait drawn by a contemporary who revered his subject and wrote to hold him up as a pattern for others.

Its importance is hard to overstate. The book was translated into Latin within a few years and swept across the Roman world. It reads almost as a manifesto: here is a way of following Christ that any believer, however unlearned, can take up. Monasteries multiplied in its wake, and the desert Antony had entered alone became crowded with imitators. Its reach even touched the conversion of the Western church’s greatest theologian: in his Confessions, Augustine of Hippo tells how hearing the story of Antony pierced him and helped drive him to his own surrender in the garden at Milan. To read Antony’s life is to read one of the most influential books the early church produced—and to sit at the source of a river that still runs.

The story Athanasius tells

Antony was born to prosperous Christian parents in Egypt and raised in the faith. Athanasius paints him as a serious boy who preferred home and church to the schoolroom—content, in the phrase the book borrows from Genesis 25:27, ‘to live a plain man at home.’ When his parents died he was about eighteen or twenty, left with a fortune and a younger sister to care for. Then, not six months later, came the moment on which everything turns. Walking to church, pondering how the apostles left all to follow Jesus, he entered just as the Gospel was being read and heard the Lord’s words to the rich man from Matthew 19:21—that to be perfect he should sell what he had and give to the poor. Antony took it as spoken directly to him. He gave away his lands, sold his goods, and kept only a little for his sister. Soon after, hearing Matthew 6:34, ‘be not anxious for the morrow,’ he gave the rest away too, placed his sister with faithful virgins, and gave himself wholly to discipline.

He began by apprenticing himself to a devout old hermit near the village and imitating every holy man he could find, ‘like the prudent bee.’ He worked with his hands, mindful of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 that the idle should not eat, and prayed constantly, taking to heart Matthew 6:6 and 1 Thessalonians 5:17. Then the conflict began in earnest. Athanasius devotes chapter after chapter to Antony’s combat with the devil—first through the memory of his wealth and family, then through lust, then through open assault. In one famous scene Antony shuts himself in a tomb, and the demons beat him until he lies as if dead; carried out senseless, he insists on being returned, and cries from the floor where he cannot even stand:

Here am I, Antony; I flee not from your stripes, for even if you inflict more nothing shall separate me from the love of Christ.

Athanasius

The line deliberately echoes Romans 8:35. From the tombs Antony withdrew farther—across the Nile to a ruined desert fort, where he lived walled in for nearly twenty years. When at last his friends broke down the door, expecting to find a wreck of a man, they were astonished: he came out whole in body and serene in soul, ‘initiated in the mysteries and filled with the Spirit of God.’ This is the hinge of the book. The hidden years of struggle had not hollowed him out; they had formed him. Now he emerged as healer, counsellor, and teacher, and disciples gathered until, in Athanasius’s memorable image, ‘cells arose even in the mountains, and the desert was colonised by monks.’ The wilderness had become a city.

The long middle of the book shows Antony as a public father: giving his great address to the monks, healing the sick and troubled, discerning spirits, counselling the anxious, refusing the Arian heresy, and answering emperors and philosophers alike with plain faith. At last, past a hundred years old, he withdrew again to his inner mountain to die. Summoning the two disciples who had attended him for fifteen years, he charged them to keep the discipline, to shun the heretics, and to remember his counsel: ‘Live as though dying daily.’ Then, Athanasius writes, ‘as though he saw friends coming to him,’ his face grew glad, and ‘he died and was gathered to the fathers.’ His body was buried in secret, at his own request, and his fame, the book insists, filled Spain, Gaul, Rome, and Africa—proof, to Athanasius, not of Antony’s cleverness but of God’s love.

The central themes

Renunciation. Everything begins with Antony hearing a command and obeying it without hedging. The book is unembarrassed that the gospel really asks for our hands to open. Yet renunciation here is not self-hatred; it is exchange. In his address Antony reasons that eternal life is bought ‘for a trifle,’ that the whole span of our years—he quotes Psalm 90:10 on our threescore years and ten—is nothing against what is promised, so that letting go of the lesser to gain the greater is only common sense.

as though making a beginning daily let us increase our earnestness. For the whole life of man is very short, measured by the ages to come, wherefore all our time is nothing compared with eternal life.

Athanasius

Spiritual warfare. Modern readers often find the demons the strangest part of the book, and we will return to that. But note first how Antony fights: never by his own strength, always by faith, prayer, fasting, and the words of Scripture flung at temptation. The devil is real and malicious in this telling, yet Athanasius is careful to insist he is also weak—‘how fierce they are, but how little power they have.’ The demons can frighten but cannot compel; the last word belongs to Christ.

Discernment. Antony’s long teaching to the monks is largely about telling true from false—which voices to trust, how to read one’s own heart, how to keep from spiritual pride. Athanasius returns again and again to Antony’s balance: neither crushed by grief nor giddy with praise, ‘altogether even as being guided by reason.’ The desert did not make him strange; it made him steady.

The desert as a place of formation. Antony does not flee to the wilderness to escape people so much as to be made whole for them. The solitude is a forge. It is telling that healing, wisdom, and gladness pour out of him only after the hidden years. And it is telling, too, that his power is always borrowed: Athanasius stresses that his cures were done ‘by Christ alone, through prayer,’ never presented as Antony’s own. The book credits every good to God—the God who, in the words Antony loved from Romans 8:32, ‘spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all.’

Who should read it

This is a short book with a long reach, and several kinds of reader will find it rewarding. Anyone curious about the roots of monasticism should start here; this is the founding document. Readers interested in church history will meet a fourth-century world—its persecutions, its Arian controversies, its hunger for holiness—through the eyes of one of its central figures. Those drawn to the spiritual life will find a bracing, uncomplicated call to take Christ’s words seriously and to give prayer the central place. And readers who love Augustine’s Confessions will want to read the book that helped set Augustine’s own heart alight.

It is also, frankly, a good book for anyone who feels the modern Christian life has grown comfortable. Antony is extreme, and he means to be. You need not copy his cave to be provoked by his single-mindedness. The book asks a question most of us would rather not answer: what are we still holding that Christ has quietly asked us to open our hands and give away?

How to read it today

The honest difficulty is that this is a very old spirituality, and parts of it will feel foreign. The demons appear as physical assailants; miracles and visions crowd the pages; the sheer severity of Antony’s life can look less like holiness than like harm. The best posture is historical sympathy—neither mocking the miraculous as primitive superstition nor swallowing every detail uncritically, but reading as Athanasius wrote: as a believer describing a believer he loved.

A few practical suggestions. First, read the demonic episodes as the text presents them—as a real spiritual struggle rendered in the vivid, embodied idiom of the ancient world—and ask what they are teaching about temptation, rather than getting stuck on the mechanics. Second, notice that Athanasius is writing hagiography, a life meant to edify; he is painting an icon, not filing a police report, and the point is the pattern of holiness, not a modern biography’s standard of proof. Third, let the strangeness do its work. The distance between Antony’s world and ours is exactly what lets him challenge our assumptions about comfort, possessions, and the seriousness of prayer. Read slowly, a chapter or two at a time; the book is short and its chapters are self-contained, so it rewards a meditative pace more than a single sitting.

Finally, read it alongside Athanasius’s great doctrinal work, On the Incarnation. The two illuminate each other beautifully: the treatise argues that God became man so that man might be remade, and the life shows what one remade man actually looked like. Antony’s deathbed charge—that his disciples ‘ever breathe Christ, and trust Him’—is the doctrine of the treatise lived out to the end. When Antony finally dies, Athanasius’s closing image is not of a grim ascetic but of a man greeting friends:

as though he saw friends coming to him and was glad because of them—for as he lay his countenance appeared joyful—he died and was gathered to the fathers.

Athanasius

For reflection

  • Antony heard Matthew 19:21 as if it were spoken to him alone and acted at once. What word of Scripture have you heard clearly but kept at arm’s length—and what would obeying it ‘today’ look like?
  • Antony’s decades of hidden struggle formed the man who later healed and counselled thousands. Where in your own life might unseen faithfulness be doing more than visible success?
  • He fought temptation with prayer, fasting, and Scripture rather than willpower. Which of these has the smallest place in your life right now, and why?
  • Athanasius insists the demons are ‘fierce’ yet have ‘little power.’ How does that double truth—taking evil seriously without fearing it—change the way you face your own temptations?
  • Antony told his disciples to ‘live as though dying daily,’ echoing 1 Corinthians 15:31. What would change this week if you took that counsel to heart?

Read on for the full text of The Life of Antony, freely available here, and let one ancient man’s wholehearted ‘yes’ sharpen your own.
